content_voiceover: This is the classic multimer gel that every boards question on von Willebrand disease references, from Ruggeri's original 1982 paper. You're looking at electrophoresis of plasma VWF, separated from high molecular weight multimers on the left down to low molecular weight on the right. Normal plasma shows a full, dense ladder across the entire range. Type 1 VWD shows the same pattern but faint throughout, because it's a purely quantitative defect, less VWF but normal multimer distribution. Type 2, subtypes A and B, shows selective loss of the high molecular weight multimers, the large bands up top are missing or reduced, while the smaller ones remain, that's the qualitative defect. Type 3 shows essentially nothing, a blank lane, because VWF is virtually absent. For boards, the pattern to memorize is quantitative loss with preserved distribution equals type 1, loss of just the large multimers equals type 2A or 2B, and complete absence equals type 3.
keypoints: Type 1: uniformly faint ladder = quantitative defect
Type 2A/2B: selective loss of HMW multimers = qualitative defect
Type 3: absent multimers, virtually no VWF
Multimer analysis distinguishes quantitative vs qualitative VWD
keypoint_voiceover: On multimer analysis, type 1 VWD shows a full but faint ladder, low quantity but normal distribution. Type 2A and 2B both show selective loss of the high molecular weight multimers while smaller ones persist, a qualitative defect. Type 3 shows a blank lane with essentially no VWF at all. This test is what separates quantitative from qualitative VWD subtypes on boards.
